nameStory: The scientific name "catulus" comes from Greek meaning "little cat," and it's easy to see why! When you look at this tiny sea slug head-on, its rounded head and the way it carries itself bears a charming resemblance to a miniature feline face.
description: The Little Cat Elysia is a small sea slug that lives in New England's coastal waters. Unlike the colorful nudibranchs you might be familiar with, this marine gastropod belongs to a different group called sacoglossans. It has a distinctive cat-like head shape that gives it its common name, and like other elysias, it has a flattened body that helps it glide along underwater surfaces.

idTips.label: Cat-like head shape
idTips.description: The rounded head with its smooth, dome-like appearance distinctly resembles a tiny cat's face when viewed from the front

idTips.label: Flattened body form
idTips.description: Body appears pressed and ribbon-like, allowing it to undulate gracefully through the water with wave-like motions

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Tiny marine slug that you'll need to look closely to spot among algae and underwater vegetation

idTips.label: Smooth texture
idTips.description: Surface lacks the elaborate projections or cerata found on true nudibranchs, appearing sleek and streamlined

habitat: Look for Little Cat Elysias in shallow coastal waters along New England's rocky shores and tide pools. They're typically found crawling on algae and seaweed in protected marine environments where they can feed undisturbed.

seasonality.spring: More active as water temperatures begin to warm, often found grazing on early spring algae growth in tide pools.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most likely to be spotted during low tide explorations of rocky intertidal zones.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may be less conspicuous as they prepare for cooler months ahead.
seasonality.winter: Least active period, though they may still be present in deeper tide pools that don't freeze.

funFact: Despite being called a sea slug, the Little Cat Elysia is more closely related to snails than to the garden slugs in your backyard - it's essentially a marine snail that has lost its shell through evolution!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with small nudibranchs, but remember that elysias have smooth, streamlined bodies while nudibranchs typically have elaborate finger-like projections or frilly appendages on their backs.
contextualKnowledge: The term "sea slug" can be confusing since these marine creatures aren't actually slugs at all - they're specialized marine snails that have evolved without shells, belonging to completely different families than terrestrial slugs.
compareHints: The Little Cat Elysia differs from its relative, the Eastern Emerald Elysia, primarily in size and the distinctive cat-like head shape that gives it its name. While both are sacoglossan sea slugs with flattened bodies, the Eastern Emerald Elysia is typically larger and lacks the pronounced feline facial resemblance that makes catulus so distinctive.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Eastern Emerald Elysia can be distinguished from its relative Elysia catulus by its brighter green coloration and more distinctly leaf-like body shape.
